comments.author: @minimalreification
comments.text:
Good interview.  A lot of what Zuckerberg said made sense. 

I especially appreciated his thesis that to protect the US "national security" against China or anyone else, it makes a hell of a lot more sense to have like a 3-6 month lead time to research and learn to handle the newest breakthroughs, courtesy of the ecosystem that has made the West the wellspring of technological development for the past 80 years, namely enthusiasts, hackers, universities, small businesses, etc, in concert with the larger industrial and commercial and governmental entities, than it does to have it all be secret and have a few companies together with the government/military making all the discoveries and breakthroughs and determining who gets to use what, and never revealing any technical and scientific details. 

That way - the "Our authoritarian system will be better and more creative than their authoritarian system"-model does not strike me as either a very safe bet nor as a society that will suit the creative, freethinking mind very well. 

His notion that a lot of people working in open-source will make it a lot more probably that weaknesses will be ferreted out and discovered before it can become a catastrophic failure rather than if an unknown amount and quality of resources is being dedicated to it by a small group of decision makers seems right to me.   

Just as anti-malware and finding weaknesses in existing systems and software is an ongoing effort needed to protect the functioning of the modern digital society, and the functioning of the immune system is an ongoing process required to protect the human organism against the continuous evolution of potential pathogens, with the integration of AI into our world it will become yet another software which will be explored by hobbyists and professionals alike, and discoveries of weaknesses, bugs and direct malware will be made and publicized and protected against.

I find this eminently likely to work in practice.

I suppose a good way to put the security on AI in a more simple understandable metaphor is comparing it to a weapon such as a rifle. If a small group of people have rifles and the majority don't, the group with rifles can use them on others, which can be good or bad, but then there will most likely be people who steal said gun or guns and use them in an evil manor against others who are nearly or completely defenseless.
On the contrary, if everyone is allowed access to rifles then it does not matter if some are stolen or used for evil, because the good people can use the other rifles still available to fight back to defend themselves and others who do not have the ability to defend themselves.
Evil people will always do evil things, so it is in the best interest of society that all people are given the opportunity to gain access to the means of defense, to gain experience with such resources, and to use them for the defense of themselves, their families, friends, and any innocent people who are incapable of defending themselves.

comments.text:
"If you disagree, leave a comment" - here goes:
A problem I see with open source is, what if we get a model that is capable of inventing weapons that we just don't want a lot of people to know how to make, because it would make humanity itself unstable. Right now, the main reason every billionaire doesn't have their own nukes just for fun is because making nukes requires a big production facility, which is obvious and the government will stop you - it is illegal. But the trend is that as technology develops, it becomes more accessible and easier/cheaper to produce. Applying that to WMDs, what if a model comes out which is capable of scientific discovery and it figures out how to make them in your basement? That might sound hypothetical, but if you apply the trend of "technological improvement => more powerful and more accessible tech" to weapons, that is the direction it leads us. Nukes are one example, but there are other types of WMDs that we don't want out there. Granted a human can discover this stuff too, but a human necessarily has a built-in moral framework that might make them just drop the project if it endangers humanity as a whole, whereas an AI just does what it's told (RLHF is easily removable with open models via fine tuning). On top of that, human scientific progress is slower and may give us more time to prepare compared to all of a sudden this thing leaks and millions of people have the blueprint. That is one of my concerns. Mark validly addresses concerns about inter-country competition, but I'm talking more about humanity as a whole.
